notes.rule:
**Sou** says who you are, and **é** says who someone else is. Both are forms of **ser**, to be.

In Brazil, you is **você**. It takes the same verb form as he and she: **você é**.

**Eu** and **você** can be left out when the verb makes it clear: **Sou um menino.**

Every noun is masculine or feminine: **um** goes with a masculine noun (**um homem**, **um menino**), **uma** with a feminine one (**uma mulher**, **uma menina**).

To say not, put **não** before the verb: **Eu não sou Tom.**

**Não é?** at the end of a sentence asks for agreement, like right?

Three ways to keep a conversation going.

**Não entendo** means I don't understand.
**Não entendi** means I didn't catch that.

**Mais devagar** asks for slower speech: **Fale mais devagar, por favor.**

**Pode repetir?** asks someone to say it again; **pode** means can you, and the next verb stays in its dictionary form: **Pode falar mais devagar?**

**Por favor** makes each one polite.

The word for the changes with the noun: **o** before a masculine noun (**o livro**), **a** before a feminine one (**a casa**). Brazilians often put it before a name too: **o Tom**, **a Mary**.

**Ele** is he and **ela** is she.

**Esse** and **essa** point at something: **esse** with a masculine noun, **essa** with a feminine one. **Isso** is that or this when no noun is named: **Isso é um livro.**

An adjective in **-o** changes to **-a** with a feminine noun (**pequeno**, **pequena**). One in **-e** stays the same (**grande**, **forte**).

A job has no **um** or **uma**: **Ele é professor.**

To ask how someone is, Portuguese uses **estar**, not **ser**: **Como você está?** and the answer is **Estou bem.**
**Como vai?** and **Tudo bem?** ask the same thing.

A man says **obrigado** and a woman says **obrigada**. The answer is **De nada**.

**Bom dia** is for the morning, **boa tarde** for the afternoon and **boa noite** for the evening and at bedtime.

**Com licença** gets someone's attention or asks to pass; **desculpe** says sorry.

A verb changes its ending with the person:
**como** is I eat and **come** is he, she or you eat
**bebo** is I drink and **bebe** is he, she or you drink
**Como** also means how.

To say what you like, use **gostar** with **de**:
**Eu gosto de leite**
**Você gosta de chá?**
The **de** is always there.

**Ter** means to have: **tenho** is I have, and **tem** is he, she or you have.

**Tem** on its own also means there is or there are, which is how Brazilians usually say it: **Tem leite?**

**Não** goes before the verb: **Não tenho cachorro.**

Two questions for words you don't know.

**Como se diz…?** asks how something is said: **Como se diz isso em português?**

**O que significa…?** and **O que quer dizer…?** both ask what a word means. **Quer dizer** is two words, wants to say, and together they mean means.

For more than one, most nouns add **-s** (**livro**, **livros**; **maçã**, **maçãs**). A noun in **-m** changes to **-ns** (**homem**, **homens**), and one in **-r** adds **-es** (**mulher**, **mulheres**).

The word for the changes too: **os** for masculine plurals, **as** for feminine ones. An adjective follows: **grande**, **grandes**; **bom**, **bons**.

**Nós somos** is we are
**vocês são** is you are, speaking to several people
**eles** and **elas são** is they are

**Temos** and **têm** are the same forms of **ter**.

An adjective agrees with its noun: **novo**, **velho** and **bonito** with a masculine noun, **nova**, **velha** and **bonita** with a feminine one. **Bom** becomes **boa**. **Jovem** doesn't change.

Most adjectives come after the noun (**um carro muito velho**).

**Muito** before an adjective means very; after a verb it means a lot. **Também** means also.

**Gostar de** can take a verb as well as a noun: **Gosto de nadar** means I like swimming. The verb stays in its dictionary form, ending in **-ar** or **-er**: **nadar**, **dançar**, **cantar**, **ler**.

With a person the ending changes: **canto** is I sing and **canta** is he, she or you sing.

**Ler** is irregular: **leio** is I read, **lê** is he, she or you read.

**Estar** says where someone or something is: **está** for one, **estão** for several, **estamos** for we.

**Em** means in, on or at. It joins with the word for the:
**em** and **o** make **no** (**no jardim**, **no banheiro**)
**em** and **a** make **na** (**na cozinha**, **na cama**)
**Em casa**, with no the, means at home.

**Aqui** is here and **lá** is there.

**Tem** says what there is: **Tem um gato na mesa.**

How you feel right now takes **estar**.

With an adjective, it agrees with the person: a man says **Estou cansado**, a woman **Estou cansada**; **feliz**, **triste** and **doente** don't change.

Hunger, thirst, sleepiness, fear, cold and heat take **estar com** and a noun, where English says to be:
**Estou com fome** (I'm hungry)
**Estou com sede** (I'm thirsty)
**Estou com sono** (I'm sleepy)
**Estou com frio** (I'm cold)

When the word won't come, say so and describe the thing.

**Estou procurando a palavra** means I'm looking for the word.
**É uma coisa para…** means it's a thing for…, followed by a verb: **É uma coisa para ler.**
**Como se chama isso?** asks what something is called.

**Não sei** means I don't know. **Sabe** with a verb asks whether someone knows how: **Você sabe nadar?**

My and your agree with the thing owned, not with the owner:
**meu** and **seu** with a masculine noun
**minha** and **sua** with a feminine one
**meus** and **minhas** for the plurals
**Seu** and **sua** usually mean your in Brazil.

For his and her, Brazilians put **dele** or **dela** after the noun:
**o pai dele** (his father)
**a casa dela** (her house)

Question words come first: **quem** (who), **o que** (what), **onde** (where), **quando** (when), **qual** (which) and **por que** (why).

**Que** before a noun means what or which: **Que livro é esse?**

Why is two words, **por que**. Because is one word, **porque**, and it starts the answer:
**Por que você está triste?**
**Porque estou cansado.**

**Onde fica…?** asks where a place is; **fica** is used for places that don't move. **Onde é…?** and **Onde está…?** are heard too.

**Perto** means near and **longe** means far.

**Tem** asks whether there is one: **Tem um hospital aqui perto?**

**De** says how you travel: **de trem**, **de ônibus**.

The numbers from three to ten don't change. Two does: **dois** with a masculine noun, **duas** with a feminine one, like **um** and **uma**.

How many is **quantos** with a masculine plural (**quantos livros**) and **quantas** with a feminine one (**quantas maçãs**).

Age uses **ter**, to have:
**Quantos anos você tem?**
**Tenho dez anos.**

A color comes after its noun and agrees with it: **vermelho**, **preto**, **branco** and **amarelo** with a masculine noun, **vermelha**, **preta**, **branca** and **amarela** with a feminine one. **Azul** and **verde** are the same for both.

**Que cor é…?** asks what color something is.

**Hoje** is today, **amanhã** tomorrow and **agora** now.

The days of the week have no capital letter, and the weekdays end in **-feira**: **segunda-feira**, **sexta-feira**. **Que dia é hoje?** asks the day.

The time is asked and told in the plural:
**Que horas são?**
**São duas horas.**

**Ir**, to go, is irregular:
**vou** is I go
**vai** is he, she or you go
**vamos** is we go, which also means let's go

To a place is **para** or **a**. **A** joins with the word for the:
**a** and **o** make **ao** (**ao parque**)
**a** and **a** make **à**, with its accent (**à escola**, **à loja**)
**Para** keeps the word for the: **para a escola**.

To describe someone, use **ter**:
**Ela tem cabelo curto** (she has short hair)
**Tenho olhos azuis** (I have blue eyes)

The adjective comes after the noun and agrees with it, so plural **olhos** take **azuis** and **verdes**. **Alto** and **baixo** describe a man, **alta** a woman.

An ache is **estar com dor**: **Estou com dor de cabeça** is I have a headache.

**A pé** means on foot.

**Como você se chama?** asks a name. The answer:
**Eu me chamo Ana.** or just **Me chamo Ana.**
**Chamar-se** is to be called, with **me** for I.

**Qual é o seu nome?** and **Meu sobrenome é Silva** ask and give the name and surname. **Muito prazer** means nice to meet you.

**O senhor** and **a senhora** are the polite you, for someone older or someone you don't know. They take the ele form, like **você**:
**A senhora é professora?**

**Apresento meu amigo** means this is my friend.

**Usar** and **vestir** both mean to wear:
**Vou usar o casaco.**

**A roupa**, clothes, is singular in Portuguese:
**A roupa é bonita.**

**As calças**, trousers, and **os óculos**, glasses, are always plural, so the verb is plural too:
**Onde estão as calças?**

Colors follow the noun and agree with it: **a saia vermelha**, **as calças azuis**.

**Como se escreve?** asks how a word is spelled. **Pode soletrar, por favor?** asks someone to spell it.

**Poder**, can, is followed straight by the other verb in its plain form: **posso cantar**, **pode soletrar**.

**Uma letra** is a letter of the alphabet.

Numbers from zero to twenty: **onze**, **doze**, **treze**, **catorze**, **quinze**, then **dezesseis**, **dezessete**, **dezoito**, **dezenove**, each one word, and **vinte**.

A phone number is read digit by digit or in pairs:
**Meu número é zero, três, onze, quinze.**

**Ligar para** and **telefonar para** both mean to phone someone:
**Vou telefonar para a Ana.**

Age takes **ter**, to have:
**Tenho vinte anos.** (I'm twenty)
**Quantos anos você tem?** asks how old someone is; **Qual é a sua idade?** asks the same more formally.

**Um mês**, **dois meses**. **A data de nascimento** is the date of birth; **nascer** is to be born.

**Quando é seu aniversário?** asks for a birthday.

Words for class: **a turma** (the class, the group), **o quadro** (the board), **a página**, **o papel**, **o exame**, **o colega** or **a colega** (a classmate).

**Estudar**, **aprender**, **perguntar** and **responder** are regular. **-ar** verbs end in **-o** for I and **-a** for **você**, **ele** and **ela** (**estudo**, **estuda**); **-er** verbs in **-o** and **-e** (**aprendo**, **aprende**).

Short phrases for checking:
**Um momento, por favor.**
**Espera aí.** or **Espera um momento.** asks someone to wait.
**Está certo?** asks if it's right; **Está errado** means it's wrong.

**Certo** and **errado** agree with the person: **Estou certo**, **Ela está errada**.

The tens: **trinta**, **quarenta**, **cinquenta**, **sessenta**, **setenta**, **oitenta**, **noventa**, then **cem** for a hundred.

Between the tens and the units comes **e**: **trinta e um**, **noventa e nove**.

**Quinhentos** is five hundred, **mil** a thousand, **um milhão** a million; **um milhão de** takes **de** before a noun: **um milhão de livros**.

**Morar em** says where you live:
**Moro em São Paulo.**
**Ela mora num apartamento.**

**Em** joins the article: **em** + **o** = **no**, **em** + **a** = **na**, **em** + **um** = **num**, **em** + **uma** = **numa**.

**A rua**, **a avenida** and **a praça** are street, avenue and square; **o código postal** is the postcode. **Perto de** means near, **longe de** far from.

**Ser** says what someone is like:
**Ele é moreno.**
**Ela é morena.**

Adjectives agree with the person: **gordo**, **gorda**; **baixo**, **baixa**; **ruivo**, **ruiva**. A word ending in **-e** is the same for both: **alegre**.

**Estar** is for how someone is just now:
**O menino está alegre.**

Nationalities agree with the person: **Sou brasileiro**, **Sou brasileira**; **mexicano**, **mexicana**.

Names of languages take no capital:
**Falo português.**
**Não falo chinês.**

Most countries take the article: **o Brasil**, **o México**, **a China**, so **em** + the article:
**Moro no México.**
**Ele mora na China.**
**Portugal** takes none.

**Quero** is I want; **Eu queria** is the polite I'd like, and is the usual way to ask in a shop:
**Eu queria um café, por favor.**

**Comprar**, to buy: **compro**, **compra**.

A quantity takes **de** before the food: **um quilo de maçãs**, **um quilo de batata**.

Opposites: **fácil** and **difícil**, **limpo** and **sujo**, **duro** and **mole**, **bom** and **mau**.

Adjectives in **-l** are the same for both genders: **fácil**, **difícil**, but **mau** has **má**.

**Ser** for what something is like, **estar** for how it is just now:
**O queijo é mole.**
**O pão está duro.**

Phrases that check you've understood:
**Claro.** (of course)
**Exatamente.** (exactly)
**É verdade?** (is it true?)
**Combinado!** means it's a deal, or agreed: **Amanhã, combinado?**

**Quanto custa?** asks how much one thing is; **Quanto custam?** asks for more than one:
**Quanto custam as maçãs?**

The money is the **real**, plural **reais**, and a **real** has a hundred **centavos**:
**Custa um real e cinquenta centavos.**

**Caro** and **barato** agree: **a camisa é cara**, **a saia é barata**.

**A conta** is the bill; **uma nota** is a banknote and **uma moeda** a coin.

A container takes **de** before what's in it: **uma garrafa de água**, **um saco de pão**.

**Todo dia** means every day:
**Leio todo dia.**
**Todos** is everyone, or all of them.

**Ou** means or and **mas** means but:
**Garrafa ou copo?**

**Em** joins the article: **no campo**, **na praia**, **no mar**, **na montanha**.

**O sol**, **o vento** and **o ar** are masculine; **a montanha**, **a planta** and **a flor** feminine.

**Tem**, there is, for what's in a place:
**Tem uma planta na mesa.**

**Que horas são?** asks the time. One o'clock takes **é**, every other hour **são**:
**É uma hora.**
**São três horas.**

**E meia** is half past (**São três e meia**), **e quinze** a quarter past, and **quinze para as dez** a quarter to ten.

At a time is **às**:
**A aula é às nove.**

**Da manhã**, **da tarde** and **da noite** say which part of the day; **meio-dia** is noon.

**Antes de** and **depois de** go before a verb in its plain form: **antes de nadar**.

When you didn't catch something:
**O quê?** (What?)
**Desculpe, não ouvi.** (Sorry, I didn't hear)
**Não ouço você.** (I can't hear you)
**Pode falar mais alto?** asks someone to speak up.

**Por quê**, with the accent, comes at the end of a sentence:
**Não sei por quê.**
At the start of a question it is **por que**, two words, no accent:
**Por que você não quer me ouvir?**

The days: **segunda**, **terça**, **quarta**, **quinta** and **sexta**, each short for **segunda-feira** and the rest, then **sábado** and **domingo**.

On a day is **na** (**no** for **sábado** and **domingo**): **na terça**, **no sábado**.

**Toda segunda** and **todos os dias** say how often; **uma vez por semana** is once a week.

**Costumo** + a verb says what you usually do:
**Costumo nadar no sábado.**

**Até terça!** means see you on Tuesday.

Months take no capital: **janeiro**, **fevereiro**, **março**.

In a month is **em**: **em julho**; in a season is **no** or **na**: **no verão**, **na primavera**.

Dates put the day first, with **de**: **cinco de março**. The first of the month is **primeiro**: **primeiro de maio**.

In Brazil the seasons are the other way round from Europe:
**Em dezembro está quente no Brasil.**

Words for where things are, each with **de** before the noun: **em cima de** (on top of), **debaixo de** and **embaixo de** (under), **atrás de** (behind), **na frente de** or **em frente a** (in front of), **ao lado de** (next to), **dentro** (inside) and **fora** (outside).

**De** joins the article: **de** + **o** = **do**, **de** + **a** = **da**: **em cima da mesa**, **debaixo do papel**.

**Isto**, **isso** and **aquilo** are this, that and that over there; **aquele**, **aquela** go with a noun.

**Sem** means without, **entre** between, **desde** since.

Colors follow the noun. Most agree (**roxo**, **roxa**), but **rosa**, **cinza** and **laranja** never change, and **marrom** only adds **-ns** for more than one: **a saia rosa**, **o carro cinza**.

**De** says what something is made of: **de plástico**, **de madeira**, **de metal**, **de vidro**, **de pano**.

Weather verbs have only the ele form: **chove** (it rains), **neva** (it snows), **vai chover**.

Ways to take a moment:
**Um momento…**
**Então…** (So…)
**Eu penso que sim** means I think so.

**Pensar**, to think: **penso**, **pensa**. **Ver**, to see:
**Posso ver isso?**
**Vamos ver.** (let's see)

Plans:
**Você vem?** (Are you coming?)
**Vamos ao cinema?** (Shall we go to the cinema?)

**Vir**, to come: **venho**, **vem**; **sair**, to go out: **saio**, **sai**; **ver**: **vejo**, **vemos**.

**A gente** means we in everyday Brazilian speech and takes the ele form:
**A gente vai ao cinema.**

**Livre** means free (not busy).

The day in order:
**Eu acordo, me levanto, tomo banho, tomo café da manhã.**

Some verbs take **me** for I: **me levanto**, **me deito**.

**Tomar** is to take or to have (**tomar banho**, **tomar café**); **almoçar**, **jantar** and **lanchar** are to have lunch, dinner and a snack.

**Fazer**: **faço**, **faz**. **Começar** and **acabar**: **começo às nove**, **acabo às cinco**.

Everyday verbs side by side. **Dar**, to give: **dou**, **dá**; **dar para** someone. **Seguir**: **sigo**. **Conseguir** (to manage to): **consigo**. **Perder**: **perco**.

**Mudar de**, to change something you have: **mudo de roupa**. **Passar**, to pass something:
**Pode passar o pão?**

**Sentar-se**, to sit: **me sento**. **Lavar**, **limpar** and **pintar** are regular **-ar** verbs.

Words on signs: **Entrada**, **Saída**, **Aberto**, **Fechado**, **Proibido nadar**.

They agree with the place: **a farmácia está aberta**, **o banco está fechado**.

**Abrir** and **fechar**: **abre às nove**, **fecha às seis**. **Os correios** (the post office) is plural.

Timetables: **o horário**, **a partida** (departure), **a chegada** (arrival).
**O ônibus sai às oito e chega às dez.** (sair and chegar)

A ticket is **uma passagem**; **uma passagem de ida** is one way, **de ida e volta** a round trip.

You travel **de**: **de avião**, **de barco**, **de ônibus**.

Free time: **jogar** is for games and sport (**jogar futebol**), **tocar** for instruments (**tocar violão**), **brincar** for children at play.

**Gostar de** + a noun or a verb:
**Gosto de natação.**
**Gosto de correr.**

**Conversar com** means to chat with someone.

Saying you're not sure:
**Acho que sim.** (I think so)
**Acho que não.** (I don't think so)
**Talvez.** (maybe)
**Não tenho certeza.** (I'm not sure)
**É possível.** (it's possible)
**Você tem certeza?** asks Are you sure?

The words of an announcement:
**Atenção, passageiros.**
**O voo** (flight), **o portão** (gate), **a plataforma** (platform), **a bagagem** (luggage, always singular), **a mala** (suitcase).

**Estar atrasado** is to be late:
**O voo está atrasado.**

**O destino** is the destination.

Instructions in a book or a class use the você command, which is the ele form of the present subjunctive: **leia** (read), **escreva** (write), **responda** (answer), **escolha** (choose), **complete**, **abra** (open), **feche** (close), **olhe** and **veja** (look), **ouça** (listen).

Never the tu form (**lê**, **escreve**) in instructions.

**Em dupla** means in pairs, **em grupo** in groups.

Directions on a map: **o norte**, **o sul**, **o leste**, **o oeste**; **em** + the article: **no norte**, **no sul**.

**Fica a** ... says how far:
**Fica a cinco quilômetros.**
**Fica a cem metros.**

**O mapa** is masculine though it ends in **-a**. **Visitar**, to visit; **a visita**, the visit.

To order politely, **Eu queria** ... (I'd like):
**Eu queria um café, por favor.**

**Pedir** is to ask for or to order: **peço** (I order), **pede** (orders):
**O que você vai pedir?**

**Uma xícara de café** is a cup of coffee, **um copo de suco** a glass of juice.

To ask for the check:
**Garçom, a conta, por favor.**
**O cardápio** and **o menu** are both the menu.

To get someone's attention:
**Com licença, você pode me ajudar?**

**Alguém** is someone or anyone:
**Alguém pode me ajudar?**
**Tem alguém aqui?** (Is anybody here?)

**Sem problema.** (No problem)

A meal in courses: **a entrada** (the starter), **o prato principal** (the main course), **a sobremesa** (dessert).

**O prato** is the plate and also the dish:
**Qual é o prato do dia?** (What's the dish of the day?)
**Um prato de arroz** (a plate of rice)

On the table: **o garfo** (fork), **a faca** (knife), **a colher** (spoon).

Rice and beans, **arroz e feijão**, go with most Brazilian meals.

Directions:
**à direita** (on the right, to the right)
**à esquerda** (on the left, to the left)
**Siga reto.** (Go straight ahead)

**Vire** (turn), **pare** (stop) and **siga** (go on) are the você command:
**Vire à esquerda na próxima esquina.**

**Na esquina** is on the corner; **para trás** is back, behind.

**Procuro** ... asks for a place:
**Com licença, procuro a farmácia.**

**Estou perdido** (a man) and **estou perdida** (a woman) both mean I am lost.

Asking to be shown:
**Você pode me mostrar o caminho?**
**Me mostre.** (Show me)

In Brazil **me** usually comes before the verb, as in **me mostre**.

How you go, with **de**: **de ônibus**, **de carro**, **de moto**, **de trem**; on foot is **a pé**.

**Pegar** is to take or catch a bus, a train or a taxi:
**Pego o ônibus para a escola.**

**Partir** is to leave:
**O trem parte às nove.**

**A primeira vez** is the first time; **primeira** is the form of **primeiro** with a feminine noun.

**Meu**, **minha** agree with the person named, not with the speaker:
**meu irmão**, **minha irmã**
**meus avós**, **minhas primas**

The masculine plural covers a mixed group: **os pais** (the parents), **os avós** (the grandparents), **os filhos** (the children).

**O namorado**, **a namorada** are boyfriend and girlfriend; **o marido** and **a esposa** husband and wife.

**Minha casa tem três quartos.** (My house has three bedrooms)

The rooms: **a sala** (the living room), **o quarto** (the bedroom), **a cozinha**, **o banheiro**.

Renting: **alugar** (to rent), **o aluguel** (the rent):
**Quanto custa o aluguel por mês?**

In the bathroom: **o chuveiro** (shower), **a pia** (sink), **a torneira** (faucet).

No article before a job after **sou** or **é**:
**Sou enfermeiro.**
**Ela é enfermeira.**

Many jobs have a form for a woman: **enfermeiro**, **enfermeira**. Some keep one form: **dentista**, **florista**, **policial**.

**Eu trabalho em um escritório.** (I work in an office)
**O chefe** is the boss; **a empresa**, the company.

**Não funciona.** (It doesn't work)
**Perdi a chave.** (I lost the key)

**Perdi** is I lost, and also I missed:
**Perdi o trem.**

In an emergency, the você command **chame** (call):
**Chame a polícia!**
**Chame uma ambulância, por favor!**

**É urgente.** (It's urgent)

The words on a form: **nome**, **sobrenome**, **data de nascimento**, **estado civil** (marital status), **sexo** or **gênero**.

Marital status agrees with the person: **solteiro**, **solteira**; **casado**, **casada**; **divorciado**, **divorciada**; **viúvo**, **viúva**.

**Masculino** and **feminino** are male and female.

**Assine aqui.** (Sign here)
In an email address, @ is **arroba**.

A letter opens with **querido** or **querida**, agreeing with the person:
**Querida Ana,**
**Querido João,**

Ways to end: **Um abraço** (a hug) to anyone, **Beijos** (kisses) to family and close friends.

**Enviar** and **mandar** both mean to send:
**Vou mandar uma mensagem para o Tom.**

After a quantity comes **de**:
**um litro de leite**
**cem gramas de queijo**

The same **de** says where something comes from: **leite de vaca** (cow's milk).

**Sal e pimenta, por favor.** (Salt and pepper, please)

**Legumes** and **vegetais** are both vegetables.

In the kitchen: **a geladeira** (the fridge), **o fogão** (the stove), **o forno** (the oven).

**Ligar** and **desligar** are to switch on and off:
**Posso ligar a luz?**
**Desligue a luz.** (the você command)

**Fazer compras** is to go shopping.

**Estou com dor de** ... says where it hurts:
**Estou com dor de cabeça.** (I have a headache)
**Estou com dor de dente.**

**Dói** is it hurts; the thing that hurts comes first:
**Meu dente dói.**

**Estou resfriado** (a man), **estou resfriada** (a woman): I have a cold.

**Tome um comprimido.** (Take a pill)

School in Brazil:
**o ensino fundamental** (elementary school)
**o ensino médio** (high school)
**o ensino superior** (college)

**Fazer um curso** is to take a course.

**Tirar** is to take or take out, and also to get a grade:
**Tiro uma nota boa em inglês.**
**Vamos tirar uma foto.**

At the hotel:
**Tenho uma reserva.** (I have a reservation)
**Um quarto duplo** (a double room), **um quarto individual** (a single room)

**A recepção** is the front desk.

**A carteira** is a wallet.

**O porquê**, one word with an accent, is the reason why:
**Não sei o porquê.**
